A sot is a person who drinks alcohol heavily and repeatedly — not just someone who got drunk at a party once, but someone for whom excessive drinking has become a defining, persistent habit. Think of it as a strong, old-fashioned word for a habitual drunkard.
Going Deeper: What Makes Someone a "Sot"

The word carries two closely linked ideas at once:

1. The habit of excessive drinking.
A sot drinks far too much, far too often. It is not an occasional lapse. It is a pattern. The drinking is so ingrained in their daily life that it has essentially taken over.

2. The mental dullness that results from it.
The word also suggests that all this drinking has left the person's mind sluggish, clouded, and blunted. A sot is not just drunk in the moment — they are perpetually in a fog. Their thinking is slow, their senses are dulled, and their judgment is poor, because alcohol has become their constant companion.

So when you call someone a sot, you are saying two things simultaneously: this person drinks too much, and this person has been stupefied by their own drinking.

"Sot" is not a neutral or clinical word. It is loaded with contempt and scorn. When someone is called a sot, the speaker is looking down on them — judging them, dismissing them, sometimes even mocking them. There can occasionally be a note of pity mixed in, but the dominant feeling is disapproval and disdain.

Compare this to the word "alcoholic," which is clinical and non-judgmental, used in medical or sympathetic contexts. "Sot" is the opposite — it is a word someone uses when they have little sympathy or respect for the person in question.

Is It a Common Word Today?

No. "Sot" is distinctly old-fashioned and literary. You will rarely hear it in everyday modern conversation. You are far more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic literature (novels, plays, poetry from centuries past)
  • Historical writing
  • Formal or deliberately stylized modern writing
  • Someone making a point of using an elevated or archaic-sounding insult

If someone uses the word "sot" in a modern context, they are almost certainly doing so deliberately, to sound literary, severe, or old-worldly.

The adjective sottish means being in the dull, stupefied state characteristic of a sot — drowsy, muddled, and insensible from heavy drinking. If a character in a novel is described as sitting in a sottish stupor, it means they are slumped and mentally absent from too much drink.

• The old nobleman had become a hopeless sot, rarely seen without a bottle in hand.
  • She looked at the sot slumped in the corner with a mixture of pity and disgust.
  • Years of excess had turned a once-brilliant man into a sot who could barely string a sentence together.
  • The innkeeper refused to serve the village sot any more wine.
A sot is someone who drinks so heavily and so constantly that they have become mentally dull and degraded by it — and the word is used with open scorn for such a person.
